paraphrase: Thus have I heard: in the city of medicine, Tanaduk ('beautiful to behold'), in a palace of five kinds of jewels surrounded by mountains on which medicines of warming and cooling power grow, the Medicine Buddha sat amid four retinues — gods, sages, non-Buddhists and Buddhists — and, entering the samādhi that dispels all illness, emanated the sage Rigpé Yeshe from his mind.
speaker: the compiler (Yilé Kyé)
translation_basis: Tibetan (paraphrase by the unit from memory; no text consulted)

paraphrase: The sage Yilé Kyé, emanated from the Buddha's speech, requests the teaching: how is the science of healing to be learned? Rigpé Yeshe answers that it has eight branches — the body, children, women's diseases, spirit afflictions, wounds, poisons, old age (rejuvenation) and virility — and is taught in four tantras.
speaker: Yilé Kyé; Rigpé Yeshe
notes: That the eight branches are listed in chapter 2 specifically is recalled with low confidence.
translation_basis: Tibetan (paraphrase by the unit from memory; no text consulted)

paraphrase: The basis: the body in health and disease. The three nyepa (rlung, mkhris pa, bad kan), the seven bodily constituents and the three excretions: in balance they sustain the body, disturbed they are disease. Rlung dwells chiefly in the lower body, mkhris pa in the middle and bad kan in the upper.
speaker: Rigpé Yeshe
translation_basis: Tibetan (paraphrase by the unit from memory; no text consulted)

paraphrase: Diagnosis is by three means: looking (above all at the tongue and the urine), touching (above all the pulse) and questioning (about causes, conditions and symptoms).
speaker: Rigpé Yeshe
translation_basis: Tibetan (paraphrase by the unit from memory; no text consulted)

paraphrase: Treatment is by four means — diet, behaviour, medicine and external therapy — applied to rlung, mkhris pa and bad kan disorders each in its own way; the gentler means come first.
speaker: Rigpé Yeshe
translation_basis: Tibetan (paraphrase by the unit from memory; no text consulted)

paraphrase: All of this is summarized in the image of three trees — of the basis, of diagnosis and of treatment — with their roots, nine trunks, forty-seven branches and two hundred and twenty-four leaves; their two flowers are health and long life, their three fruits Dharma, wealth and happiness.
speaker: Rigpé Yeshe
translation_basis: Tibetan (paraphrase by the unit from memory; no text consulted)
